lead: A current mirror takes a reference current and copies it into another branch. The copy is set by transistor geometry and by the shared base or gate voltage. It exists because an IC cannot afford a precise resistor for every bias current, but it can match two nearby transistors. Mirrors bias differential pairs, supply active loads, and set op-amp internal currents. A simple BJT mirror copies with a small base-current error; a MOSFET mirror copies by width-to-length ratio. Cascode and Wilson versions raise output resistance so the copy changes less when the output voltage moves.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for the tail current source, and Unit 2 for BJT and MOSFET bias circuits.

blocks.text: Connect the collector of Q<sub>1</sub> to its base. Q<sub>1</sub> is diode-connected: it has two terminals and sits at the base-emitter voltage V<sub>BE</sub> needed for the reference current. A resistor R from the positive supply V<sub>CC</sub> sets that current. Q<sub>2</sub> is a matched transistor with the same V<sub>BE</sub>. If both transistors stay in the active region, Q<sub>2</sub> copies Q<sub>1</sub>'s collector current. The circuit is a current mirror. Some syllabi call these current mirror circuits; the name is the same.

blocks.where: I<sub>REF</sub> is the reference current in amperes; V<sub>CC</sub> is the positive supply in volts; V<sub>BE</sub> is the base-emitter voltage of Q<sub>1</sub> in volts; R is the reference resistor in ohms.

blocks.text: The copy is not perfect. The reference current has to supply the collector of Q<sub>1</sub> and the base currents of both transistors. For matched devices, I<sub>REF</sub> = I<sub>OUT</sub>(1 + 2/β), where β is the common-emitter current gain. Rearrange: I<sub>OUT</sub> = I<sub>REF</sub> / (1 + 2/β). With β = 100 the error is about 2 percent. Emitter resistors improve matching because a small resistor drops a voltage that corrects small V<sub>BE</sub> differences; the cost is extra voltage headroom.

blocks.where: I<sub>OUT</sub> is the copied collector current in amperes; I<sub>REF</sub> is the reference current in amperes; β is the BJT current gain, dimensionless.

blocks.text: The output transistor must stay active. The compliance voltage is the minimum output voltage VOUT that keeps Q2 out of saturation. For a simple BJT mirror, VOUT ≥ VCE,sat, about 0.2 V to 0.3 V. Below that value the copy falls. A mirror often feeds the tail of the differential pair in 5.1. That tail current must stay fixed when the input common voltage moves, so the mirror's output resistance matters.

A current source should give the same current for any output voltage. A simple mirror does not: its output resistance is finite. For a BJT, r<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>A</sub> / I<sub>C</sub>, where V<sub>A</sub> is the Early voltage and I<sub>C</sub> is the collector current. For a MOSFET, r<sub>o</sub> = 1 / (λ I<sub>D</sub>), where λ is the channel-length modulation parameter and I<sub>D</sub> is the drain current. A larger r<sub>o</sub> means a better current source.

The Wilson mirror and the cascode mirror raise output resistance by stacking transistors and using local feedback. The cascode keeps the output device's drain or collector voltage nearly fixed, so its current changes less when V<sub>OUT</sub> moves. These mirrors need a larger compliance voltage because more devices sit in the stack. Use them when the copy must be stable, not when the available headroom is tiny.

The Widlar source gives a small output current without a small reference current. It puts a resistor R<sub>2</sub> in the emitter of the output device. The relation is I<sub>OUT</sub> R<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>T</sub> ln(I<sub>REF</sub> / I<sub>OUT</sub>), where V<sub>T</sub> ≈ 26 mV at room temperature. The current is set by R<sub>2</sub> and a logarithmic ratio, so a few microamperes are practical. Its output resistance is lower than a cascode's, so check the application.

In a MOSFET mirror, Q<sub>1</sub> is diode-connected: gate tied to drain. Q<sub>2</sub> shares the same gate-source voltage V<sub>GS</sub>. If both devices stay in saturation, the current ratio follows the width-to-length ratio: I<sub>OUT</sub> / I<sub>REF</sub> = (W/L)<sub>2</sub> / (W/L)<sub>1</sub>. Here W is channel width, L is channel length, and W/L is dimensionless. A wider Q<sub>2</sub> copies a larger current. Do not invert the ratio.

blocks.where: I<sub>OUT</sub> is the copied drain current in amperes; I<sub>REF</sub> is the reference current in amperes; (W/L)<sub>1</sub> and (W/L)<sub>2</sub> are the width-to-length ratios of Q<sub>1</sub> and Q<sub>2</sub>, dimensionless.

blocks.text: Channel-length modulation makes the copy depend on the drain-source voltage V<sub>DS</sub>. The output resistance is r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λ I<sub>D</sub>), where λ is the channel-length modulation parameter in V<sup>−1</sup>. The compliance voltage of a simple MOSFET mirror is V<sub>OUT</sub> ≥ V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TH</sub>, the overdrive voltage. Below it, Q<sub>2</sub> leaves saturation and the copy falls. A cascode MOSFET mirror raises r<sub>o</sub> but needs about one more overdrive voltage of headroom.

A mirror is the usual tail bias for a differential pair. It turns one reference current into a stable tail current. It also sets bias currents inside op-amps; the full bias chain is in 5.5. Using a mirror as an active load is a separate idea, covered in 5.4.

figure.caption: A 1 mA reference flows through diode-connected Q1 and sets VBE; matched Q2 copies about 0.9804 mA. Notice the copy is slightly lower because the reference also supplies base currents.

spec.title: Basic current mirror
spec.aria: Block diagram: a 1 mA reference current flows through diode-connected Q1, sets a base-emitter voltage, and drives a matched Q2 that copies about 0.9804 mA to the output.

examples.question: Using a 5 V supply, design a simple BJT current mirror for an output current of about 1 mA. V<sub>BE</sub> = 0.7 V, β = 100, V<sub>A</sub> = 50 V. Find R for I<sub>REF</sub> = 1 mA, the actual I<sub>OUT</sub>, and r<sub>o</sub>. State the compliance limit.
steps: Set the reference current: I<sub>REF</sub> = 1 mA. R = (V<sub>CC</sub> − V<sub>BE</sub>) / I<sub>REF</sub> = (5 V − 0.7 V) / 1 mA = 4.3 kΩ.
Apply the base-current error: I<sub>OUT</sub> = I<sub>REF</sub> / (1 + 2/β) = 1 mA / (1 + 2/100) = 1 mA / 1.02 = 0.98039 mA ≈ 0.9804 mA.
Find output resistance: r<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>A</sub> / I<sub>OUT</sub> = 50 V / 0.98039 mA = 51.0 kΩ.
Compliance: keep V<sub>OUT</sub> ≥ V<sub>CE,sat</sub>, about 0.2 V to 0.3 V. Below this value Q<sub>2</sub> saturates and the copy drops.
examples.answer: R = 4.3 kΩ, I<sub>OUT</sub> ≈ 0.9804 mA, and r<sub>o</sub> ≈ 51.0 kΩ; the output must stay above about 0.2 V.
examples.check:
VCC = 5.0
VBE = 0.7
beta = 100.0
VA = 50.0
IREF_mA = 1.0
R_kohm = (VCC - VBE) / IREF_mA
IOUT_mA = IREF_mA / (1 + 2 / beta)
ro_kohm = VA / IOUT_mA
print(f"{R_kohm:.1f}")
print(f"{IOUT_mA:.4f}")
print(f"{ro_kohm:.1f}")

traps: Treating I<sub>OUT</sub> as exactly I<sub>REF</sub> and forgetting the base-current error 2/β.
Expecting I<sub>OUT</sub> to stay fixed when V<sub>OUT</sub> changes; a real mirror has finite r<sub>o</sub>.
Inverting the MOSFET ratio; I<sub>OUT</sub>/I<sub>REF</sub> equals (W/L)<sub>2</sub>/(W/L)<sub>1</sub>.
Forgetting the compliance voltage; below V<sub>CE,sat</sub> or the overdrive the copy falls.
Confusing a Widlar source with a simple mirror: the Widlar uses an emitter resistor to get a small current.

quiz.a: A BJT with collector tied to base. It behaves as a two-terminal device whose base-emitter voltage sets its collector current.

quiz.q: Why is the simple mirror output smaller than I<sub>REF</sub>?
quiz.a: The reference current includes the base currents of both transistors. For matched devices I<sub>OUT</sub> = I<sub>REF</sub>/(1+2/β).

quiz.q: A MOSFET mirror has I<sub>REF</sub> = 100 µA, (W/L)<sub>1</sub> = 10, (W/L)<sub>2</sub> = 50. Find I<sub>OUT</sub>.
Why does a cascode mirror hold its output current more constant than a simple mirror?
quiz.a: It raises output resistance by keeping the output device voltage nearly fixed, so changes in V<sub>OUT</sub> cause smaller current changes.

quiz.q: A BJT mirror has I<sub>REF</sub> = 2 mA and β = 50. Find I<sub>OUT</sub>.
Define compliance voltage for a current mirror.
quiz.a: The minimum output voltage that keeps the output transistor in the active or saturation region, so the mirror still copies current.

quiz.q: Why is a high-output-resistance mirror useful as the tail source of a differential pair?
quiz.a: It keeps the tail current nearly constant when the common-mode input moves, which improves common-mode rejection and bias stability.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real ICs, current mirrors are laid out with matched fingers and dummy devices so that process gradients do not spoil the ratio. Precision copies use trimming, cascodes, or feedback around a reference. Data converters, bandgap references, and sensor front ends depend on stable current sources. Search next for "current mirror mismatch", "cascode current source", and "bandgap reference".
